Laying out the street

Proposed for charlierogers.art, Learning

Step inside Charlie's Gateshead

Charlie painted these streets before the bulldozers reached them. Now children can walk down them, in his colours and his ink, and see what stands there today.

The idea

The streets are gone. His paintings are the only way back into them. So let's open the door.

Using the newest 3D tools, Charlie's street paintings become small worlds a child can walk around on a school laptop or tablet. Not a photograph, not a game in a modern style: his brushwork, his skies, his corner shops, with room to turn round and look down the road he was standing in.

A visit

What a class does inside a painting

A lesson from start to finish: the class together first, then into a pupil's tablet and down the street. About ten minutes per painting.

The streets

Work in progress

Five streets, as the test builds stand today

These are early working builds, made from the paintings alone to prove the idea. Pick a street, press step inside, and drag to look around. They are rough in places on purpose: the final build fixes what you see here.

What you will notice

  • Walls seen side-on stretch and smear as you walk past them, most on Cotfield Street's left terrace and the yard wall in Third Street.
  • Walk to the far end of a street and it softens into wash.
  • The gaps behind people are filled automatically for now.

What the final build does

  • The hidden sides of buildings and the gaps behind people are painted by hand in Charlie's palette, so his paint holds as you pass instead of stretching.
  • Every painting separated into clean layers: sky, buildings, road and people.
  • Tested on school iPads, phones and laptops.

What already works

  • One engine runs all five; a new painting is a page of measurements, not new code.
  • His ink line and paper over everything.
  • Snow, chimney smoke, and people standing where their feet touch the ground.

Today

How they are made

From the painting itself

We measure each painting's perspective, build the street as simple 3D shapes and wrap Charlie's own paint around them. The people are cut out and stand in the road, and where the painting stops, the gaps are filled in his colours and ink line.

That means separating every painting into layers: sky, buildings, road and people. It is the careful part of the work, and it is what makes the rest of the site better too.

Why it matters

Modern, and still his

It would set Charlie's site apart from any other Northern artist's. It puts Charlie in front of a generation who never saw these streets, and gives the Historic England scheme of work something to send pupils to.

It also makes the story of the book physical. You feel what was lost when you walk down a street and then watch it change.

Labelled honestlyEvery world says "imagined from Charlie's painting" and links to the original.
Safe for childrenNo sign-in, no chat, nothing collected inside the worlds.
Works in classRuns on school laptops and iPads, with a simpler 360 view and a short film as backups.
Your approvalNothing goes live without yours and the family's say-so.

Around it

A home for the Historic England scheme of work

The worlds sit inside a learning hub that does justice to Andrew Wrenn's scheme, with your text, your photograph of Charlie and the pupils' paintings you sent.

A walking route to the places he painted, built on the site's map, with a printable sheet for a class outing.

How many schools have downloaded the scheme, in your admin. The figures Historic England and funders ask for.

Investment

Stage 2 of charlierogers.art

Start with five streets for £600. Separating the paintings into layers also lifts the main website, so this is the next stage of the site as well as a new feature for schools.
